authoredSolutions.1: The third member of the Lyman series is the \(n = 4 \rightarrow 1\) transition: \[\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}} = R\left( 1 - \frac{1}{16} \right) = \frac{15R}{16} \Rightarrow \lambda_{1} = \frac{16}{15R}\] The first member of the Paschen series is \(n = 4 \rightarrow 3\): \[\frac{1}{\lambda_{2}} = R\left( \frac{1}{9} - \frac{1}{16} \right) = \frac{7R}{144} \Rightarrow \lambda_{2} = \frac{144}{7R}\] \[\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{2}} = \frac{16}{15} \times \frac{7}{144} = \frac{7}{135}\] so \(\lambda_{1}:\lambda_{2} = 7:135\).
authoredSolutions.2: In the steady state the same heat current flows through both sheets: \[\frac{\theta_{1} - \theta}{R_{1}} = \frac{\theta - \theta_{2}}{R_{2}}\] \[R_{2}\left( \theta_{1} - \theta \right) = R_{1}\left( \theta - \theta_{2} \right) \Rightarrow \theta\left( R_{1} + R_{2} \right) = \theta_{1}R_{2} + \theta_{2}R_{1}\] \[\theta = \frac{\theta_{1}R_{2} + \theta_{2}R_{1}}{R_{1} + R_{2}}\]

authoredSolutions.4: Resolving power is limited by the wavelength used: the smallest resolvable separation scales with \(\lambda\). Electrons accelerated through an electron gun have a de Broglie wavelength of the order of picometres, thousands of times shorter than the \(400 - 700\text{ nm}\) of visible light, so an electron microscope resolves far finer detail. Both statements are true, and the short de Broglie wavelength is precisely the reason for the better resolving power, so R is the correct explanation of A.

authoredSolutions.25: The quality factor of a series LCR circuit at resonance is \[Q = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}\] Doubling \(L\) and halving \(R\) gives \[Q' = \frac{1}{R/2}\sqrt{\frac{2L}{C}} = 2\sqrt{2} \times \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = 2\sqrt{2}\,Q\] \[Q' = 2\sqrt{2} \times 100 = 282.84\]
authoredSolutions.72: The line \(x-y=0\) has slope \(1\); \(x+2y=3\) has slope \(-\frac{1}{2}\); \(2x+y=6\) has slope \(-2\). The acute angle between the first and second satisfies \(\tan\theta=\left|\frac{1-(-1/2)}{1+1\cdot(-1/2)}\right|=3\), and between the first and third \(\tan\theta=\left|\frac{1-(-2)}{1+1\cdot(-2)}\right|=3\). Two equal angles make the triangle isosceles. Hence (C).
authoredSolutions.81:
Substitute \(u=x-1\), so the curve becomes \(y=\big||u|-2\big|\); the answer is the same because a horizontal shift does not change area.

Find where the curve meets \(y=2\): \(\big||u|-2\big|=2\Rightarrow |u|-2=\pm 2\Rightarrow |u|=4\) or \(|u|=0\). So the line touches the curve at \(u=-4,\ 0,\ 4\).

On \([0,4]\): for \(0\le u\le 2\), \(y=2-u\); for \(2\le u\le 4\), \(y=u-2\). The curve dips to \(y=0\) at \(u=2\) and rises back to \(y=2\) at \(u=4\). By symmetry the shape on \([-4,0]\) is the mirror image, so the required area is
\[\text{Area}=2\int_{0}^{4}\big(2-y\big)\,du.\]

Compute the two pieces:
\[\int_{0}^{2}\big(2-(2-u)\big)\,du=\int_{0}^{2}u\,du=2,\qquad \int_{2}^{4}\big(2-(u-2)\big)\,du=\int_{2}^{4}(4-u)\,du=\Big[4u-\tfrac{u^{2}}{2}\Big]_{2}^{4}=8-6=2.\]

Thus \(\int_{0}^{4}(2-y)\,du=2+2=4\), and the total area \(=2\times 4=8.\)
